docs.title: LTRCLD-1199 – Using Containers on Cisco Edge Devices to Turbocharge Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Welcome to LTRCLD-1199, a hands-on lab for deploying and operating containerized troubleshooting tools on Cisco IOS-XE (Catalyst 8000v / C8Kv) using:

  • Native App-Hosting
  • Terraform (Infrastructure as Code)
  • Kubernetes (kind + Virtual Kubelet)

docs.title: Lab Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

  • Deploy a containerized tool on C8Kv using App-Hosting via CLI
  • Automate App-Hosting configuration with Terraform
  • Integrate C8Kv into a Kubernetes environment using kind and Virtual Kubelet
  • Validate that tools are running and accessible for troubleshooting work

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
To get the most value from this lab, you should be familiar with:

  • Basic IOS-XE CLI navigation
  • Fundamentals of Docker containers
  • Basic understanding of Terraform and/or YAML
  • Very basic Kubernetes concepts (Pods, Nodes) — helpful but not required

docs.title: 🔧 Swiss-Knife Container (Primary Troubleshooting Toolkit)
docs.text:
The Swiss-Knife container is the core operational tool in this lab.

It bundles a wide range of commonly used CLI utilities into a single lightweight Alpine-based image, allowing engineers to perform most troubleshooting tasks without deploying multiple containers.

Typical use cases

  • Connectivity and reachability validation
  • Performance and throughput testing
  • Application-level troubleshooting
  • Traffic generation and inspection
  • Telemetry and metrics export

Included tools

  • Connectivity & diagnostics: ping, traceroute, mtr, fping, telnet, ssh
  • Traffic & performance: iperf3, tcpdump, socat
  • Network discovery & testing: nmap, net-tools, iproute2
  • Messaging & streaming: kcat
  • Telemetry & monitoring: telegraf
  • SNMP & DNS utilities: net-snmp-tools, bind-tools
  • Automation & parsing: curl, wget, httpie, jq, yq, python3
  • General utilities: nano, tcsh, whois

Design philosophy: One container, many tools – optimized for fast troubleshooting and reduced operational overhead.

In our lab the contianer is deployed on two routers:

  • Cat8Kv-task-1 with IP 198.18.100.5
  • Cat8Kv-task-2 with IP 198.18.101.5

docs.title: 🦈 Wireshark Container (Deep Packet Inspection)
docs.text:
The Wireshark container is used for advanced packet-level visibility.

It is deployed as a dedicated analysis tool, receiving mirrored traffic (e.g. ERSPAN) from the router and decoding it using Wireshark’s rich protocol dissectors.

Typical use cases

  • ERSPAN-based traffic analysis
  • Application and protocol troubleshooting
  • Packet-level validation of control and data planes

Why separate? Packet analysis requires elevated capabilities and a focused runtime. Keeping Wireshark isolated avoids unnecessary overhead in the Swiss-Knife container.

In our lab this contianer is deployed on one router:

  • Cat8Kv-task-2 with IP 198.18.101.6

docs.title: 📈 MRTG Container (SNMP-Based Monitoring)
docs.text:
The MRTG container provides classic SNMP polling and graphing, ideal for visualizing long-term interface and device statistics.

Key components

  • mrtg + rrdtool for time-series graph generation
  • net-snmp-tools for polling and validation
  • lighttpd to serve generated graphs over HTTP
  • dcron for scheduled data collection

Typical use cases

  • Interface bandwidth trending
  • SNMP validation and demos
  • Simple, self-contained monitoring dashboards

Note: MRTG is intentionally kept separate from Telegraf-based telemetry to demonstrate different monitoring models side-by-side.

In our lab this contianer is deployed on one router:

  • Cat8Kv-task-1 with IP 198.18.100.6

docs.text: Container Primary Role Key Strength Swiss-Knife Day-to-day troubleshooting All-in-one CLI toolkit Wireshark Packet capture & protocol analysis Deep visibility MRTG SNMP polling & graphing Simple historical trends

This task focuses on deploying a containerized troubleshooting application on a Cisco IOS-XE router using the App-Hosting feature.

The process includes:

  • Pulling the image from a container registry
  • Converting the image to a TAR package
  • Copying the image to the router using SCP
  • Installing and activating the application using App Hosting
  • Testing the deployed application
  • We will deploy two containers in this task

docs.title: Step 1: Check Container Registry and retrieve image

• Login to the Lab Ubuntu (ssh 198.18.1.100)
  • Check the docker registry
  • Pull the swiss-knife and mrtg image from a container registry
    • This image will be used to create a TAR file for router deployment
curl -s https://containers.dmz.cisco.com:5000/v2/_catalog

dcloud@ubuntu-lab:~$ curl -s https://containers.dmz.cisco.com:5000/v2/_catalog
{"repositories":["hello-app","mrtg","swiss-knife-alpine","wireshark"]}

sudo docker pull containers.dmz.cisco.com:5000/swiss-knife-alpine:latest

sudo docker pull containers.dmz.cisco.com:5000/mrtg:latest

Verify the image was downloaded:

dcloud@ubuntu-lab:~$ sudo docker images

docs.text:
• Convert the Docker image into a TAR archive
    • This file will be transferred to the router
sudo docker save containers.dmz.cisco.com:5000/swiss-knife-alpine:latest -o swiss-knife-alpine.tar

sudo docker save containers.dmz.cisco.com:5000/mrtg:latest -o mrtg.tar

Verify the TAR file exists:

ls -lh swiss-knife-alpine.tar
ls -lh mrtg.tar

docs.title: Step 3: SCP File to cat8Kv-task-1
docs.text:
• Login to cat8Kv-task-1 using 198.18.1.11
  • Enable SCP server
conf t
ip scp server enable
end
  • Copy the TAR image from your lab ubuntu to the router
sudo scp swiss-knife-alpine.tar admin@198.18.1.11:/flash:/swiss-knife-alpine.tar

Verify the file on the router:

dir bootflash: | include swiss-knife-alpine.tar

The file output should look like this: 

cat8Kv-task-1#dir bootflash: | include swiss-knife-alpine.tar
13      -rw-        400191488   Feb 3 2026 13:57:13 +00:00  swiss-knife-alpine.tar

docs.title: Step 5: App-Hosting Configuration on cat8kv-task-1
docs.text:
• Login to cat8Kv-task-1 using 198.18.1.11
  • Enable IOx application framework
  • Create a virtual interface for the container and advertise in OSPF
  • Configure network connectivity for the application
  • Allocate IP address and gateway for the container
conf t

 iox

 int virtualportgroup0
 ip address 198.18.100.1 255.255.255.0
 ip ospf 1 area 0

app-hosting appid swiss_knife
 app-vnic gateway0 virtualportgroup 0 guest-interface 0
  guest-ipaddress 198.18.100.5 netmask 255.255.255.0
 app-default-gateway 198.18.100.1 guest-interface 0
 name-server0 8.8.8.8

end

Verify configuration:

show run | sec app-hosting

docs.title: Step 6: App-Hosting Install on cat8kv-task-1
docs.text:
• Install the application from the TAR file
  • This step extracts and prepares the container
  • Enable terminal monitor to see the logs for progress
app-hosting install appid swiss_knife package bootflash:swiss-knife-alpine.tar

In case the following error is seen, 

ioxman: app-hosting: Failed to install swiss_knife: App signature validation is required. App signature file package.cert or package.sign not found in package

Enable and disable App-Hosting signature verification and run the install command again.

conf t
app-hosting signed-verification
end

conf t
no app-hosting signed-verification
end

*Jan 13 12:00:35.447: %IM-6-VERIFICATION_MSG: R0/0: ioxman: app-hosting: App signature verification disabled successfully

Validate installation:

show app-hosting detail appid swiss_knife

app-hosting activate appid swiss_knife

Verify state:

This task uses iperf3 inside the Swiss-Knife container to validate throughput, directionality, parallelism, UDP behavior, and MTU impact between two Catalyst 8000v routers.

You will run: - iperf3 server on cat8Kv-task-2 - iperf3 client on cat8Kv-task-1

docs.title: 1. Topology and Roles
docs.text:
Node Role Container IP Address cat8Kv-task-1 Client swiss_knife Connects to 198.18.101.5 cat8Kv-task-2 Server swiss_knife Listens on 198.18.101.5

Note: Update the IP address if your server-side container uses a different value.

docs.title: 2. Start iPerf3 Server (cat8Kv-task-2)
docs.text:
2.1 Connect to the Swiss-Knife container:

app-hosting connect appid swiss_knife session /bin/bash

2.2 Start iPerf3 in server mode:

iperf3 -s

docs.title: What to verify
docs.text:
• Output shows: Server listening on 5201
  • Server displays connection statistics when tests run
  • If no connection is seen:
  • Verify IP reachability between containers
  • Confirm no ACL, NAT, or firewall blocks TCP/5201

docs.title: 3.1 Connect to the Swiss-Knife container:
docs.text: app-hosting connect appid swiss_knife session /bin/bash

docs.title: 3.2 Basic TCP throughput (client → server):
docs.text: iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5

docs.title: What to verify
docs.text:
• Note the receiver throughput in the final summary
  • This represents effective end-to-end performance

docs.title: 3.3 Reverse direction throughput (server → client):
docs.text: iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5 -R

docs.title: What to verify
docs.text:
• Compare results with step 3.2

  • Large differences may indicate:

  • Directional QoS or policing

  • CPU constraints on one node
  • Asymmetric routing

docs.title: 3.4 Parallel TCP streams:
docs.text: iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5 -P 5

docs.title: What to verify
docs.text:
• Aggregate throughput should increase vs single stream

  • If throughput decreases:

  • Check CPU utilization

  • Check congestion or drops in the path

docs.title: 3.5 Short-duration TCP test:
docs.text: iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5 -t 5

docs.title: 3.6 Long-duration TCP test:
docs.text: iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5 -t 60

docs.title: What to verify
docs.text:
• Throughput consistency over time
  • Degradation over long runs may indicate:
  • Traffic shaping
  • Buffer exhaustion
  • Sustained CPU load

docs.title: 4.1 UDP test at 100 Mbps:
docs.text: iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5 -u -b 100M

docs.title: What to verify
docs.text:
• Packet loss should be minimal in a clean lab
  • Observe jitter and packet loss percentage

docs.title: 4.2 UDP test at 50 Mbps with 1400-byte packets:
docs.text: iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5 -u -b 50M -l 1400

docs.title: 4.3 UDP test at 50 Mbps with 1470-byte packets:
docs.text: iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5 -u -b 50M -l 1470

docs.title: 4.4 UDP test at 50 Mbps with 1510-byte packets:
docs.text: iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5 -u -b 50M -l 1510

docs.title: What to verify
docs.text:
• Packet loss appearing only at larger sizes indicates MTU mismatch
  • Consistent loss at all sizes suggests congestion or policing

docs.title: 5.1 Run iPerf3 with JSON output:
docs.text: iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5 -J

docs.title: 5.2 Short-duration JSON output:
docs.text: iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5 -t 5 -J

docs.title: 5.3 Extract received throughput using jq:
docs.text: iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5 -t 5 -J | jq '.end.sum_received.bits_per_second'

docs.title: What to verify
docs.text:
• JSON output is useful for automation and dashboards
  • Values are returned in raw bits per second
  • Results can be stored for later analysis:
iperf3 -c 198.18.101.5 -t 10 -J > iperf_result.json

docs.title: 6.1 Connectivity
docs.text:
• Verify container-to-container ping
  • Validate routing between VirtualPortGroup interfaces
  • Confirm TCP/5201 and UDP traffic is permitted

docs.title: 6.2 Performance Symptoms and Causes
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Low TCP, good UDP TCP windowing or single-flow hashing Reverse slower than forward QoS or policing asymmetry UDP loss at low rate Congestion or shaping Loss only with large packets MTU mismatch

docs.title: 7. Key iperf3 Options Reference
docs.text: Option Description -s Server mode -c IP Client mode -R Reverse direction -P N Parallel streams -u UDP mode -b RATE UDP bandwidth -t SEC Test duration -l BYTES Packet length -J JSON output --logfile FILE Save output to file

docs.title: 8. Expected Outcome
docs.text:
By completing this task, you should be able to:

  1. Validate TCP throughput between C8Kv-hosted containers
  2. Identify directional asymmetry in the data path
  3. Demonstrate the impact of parallel flows
  4. Measure UDP loss and jitter
  5. Detect MTU mismatches using packet-size variation
  6. Generate machine-readable performance metrics

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:

  • Step 2 – Enable Packet Capture Permissions (One-Time Fix)
  • Step 3 – Restart the Wireshark Application
  • Step 4 – Configure ERSPAN on Cat8Kv-Task-1
  • Step 5 – Access the Wireshark Web GUI

  • Step 8 – Observe the Live Capture
  • What You Have Demonstrated

In this task, you will use Wireshark running inside a container to perform live packet capture from a remote router interface using ERSPAN.

This demonstrates how App-Hosting on Cisco edge devices can be used for real-time traffic visibility without deploying external probes.

docs.title: Task Overview
docs.text:
• Wireshark container is deployed on Cat8Kv-Task-2
  • SSH traffic on Cat8Kv-Task-1 (GigabitEthernet6) is mirrored using ERSPAN
  • Mirrored packets are sent to the Wireshark container
  • Traffic is analyzed live using the Wireshark Web GUI

docs.title: Step 1 – Connect to the Wireshark Container
docs.text:
Login to Cat8Kv-Task-2 and connect to the Wireshark container shell.

app-hosting connect appid wireshark session /bin/bash

You should now be inside the container.

docs.title: Step 2 – Enable Packet Capture Permissions (One-Time Fix)
docs.text:
Wireshark GUI uses a helper binary called dumpcap to capture packets. By default, it does not have the required Linux capabilities inside the container.

Run the following commands inside the container:

sudo -i

which dumpcap

setcap cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin=eip /usr/bin/dumpcap

getcap /usr/bin/dumpcap

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
• sudo -i # Switches to root inside the container.

  • which dumpcap # Confirms the location of the packet capture binary.

  • setcap cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin=eip /usr/bin/dumpcap # Grants packet capture permissions without running Wireshark as root.

  • getcap /usr/bin/dumpcap # Verifies that the permissions are applied correctly.

Expected output:

/usr/bin/dumpcap = cap_net_admin,cap_net_raw+eip

docs.title: Step 3 – Restart the Wireshark Application
docs.text:
Exit the wireshark container and restart the application so the new permissions take effect.

app-hosting stop appid wireshark

app-hosting start appid wireshark

docs.title: Step 4 – Configure ERSPAN on Cat8Kv-Task-1
docs.text: On Cat8Kv-Task-1, configure ERSPAN to mirror SSH traffic (TCP port 22) from GigabitEthernet6.

docs.title: 4.1 Create an ACL to Match SSH Traffic
docs.text:
ip access-list extended 100
 10 permit tcp any any eq 22

docs.title: 4.2 Configure ERSPAN Source Session
docs.text:
monitor session 11 type erspan-source
 no shutdown
 source interface GigabitEthernet6
 filter access-group 100
 destination
  erspan-id 11
  mtu 1464
  ip address 198.18.101.6

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
In this task, you deploy and extend a Telegraf-based monitoring probe running inside the swiss-knife container to demonstrate how modern telemetry pipelines can be built on edge devices.

You will:

  • Collect container self-metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network)
  • Perform ICMP reachability and HTTP/HTTPS availability checks
  • Expose metrics via a Prometheus /metrics endpoint
  • Extend the same probe to collect router metrics using SNMP
  • Visualize both container and router metrics centrally using Prometheus and Grafana

docs.title: 3.2 Virtual Kubelet Deployment
docs.text:
File: 03_vk_deployment-r1.yaml

cat > 03_vk_deployment-r1.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cisco-virtual-kubelet-r1
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: cisco-virtual-kubelet-r1
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cisco-virtual-kubelet-r1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cisco-virtual-kubelet-r1
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/hostname: ubuntu-lab
      containers:
      - name: virtual-kubelet
        image: containers.dmz.cisco.com:5000/cisco-virtual-kubelet:1.0.0
        env:
        - name: KUBECONFIG
          value: "/etc/kubernetes/kubeconfig.yaml"
        volumeMounts:
        - name: kubeconfig-storage
          mountPath: "/etc/kubernetes"
          readOnly: true
        - name: vk-config-storage
          mountPath: "/etc/virtual-kubelet"
          readOnly: true
      volumes:
      - name: kubeconfig-storage
        configMap:
          name: remote-kubeconfig
          items:
          - key: "config"
            path: "kubeconfig.yaml"
      - name: vk-config-storage
        configMap:
          name: vk-config-r1
          items:
          - key: "config.yaml"
            path: "config.yaml"
EOF

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: In this task, you will configure passwordless SSH access from the ubuntu-lab host to multiple Catalyst 8000v (Cat8Kv) routers using SSH public key authentication. This enables secure, automation-friendly access without interactive password prompts.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Ubuntu host with user dcloud
  • SSH client installed (default on Ubuntu)
  • Administrative access to Cat8Kv routers

docs.title: Step 1: Create SSH Key on Ubuntu
docs.text:
Log in to the Ubuntu system and switch to the dcloud user:

su - dcloud

Generate an RSA SSH key pair:

ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 1024 -f ~/.ssh/c8kv_admin_key

When prompted for a passphrase, press Enter to leave it empty (or set one if required).

This creates the following files:

  • ~/.ssh/c8kv_admin_key – Private key
  • ~/.ssh/c8kv_admin_key.pub – Public key

docs.title: Step 2: Copy Public Key from Ubuntu
docs.text:
Display the public key:

cat ~/.ssh/c8kv_admin_key.pub

Example output:

ssh-rsa AAAAB3NzaC1yc2EAAAADAQABAAACAQ... dcloud@ubuntu

Copy the entire line, including ssh-rsa and the comment at the end.

docs.title: Step 3: Configure SSH Public Key on Cat8Kv Routers
docs.text:
Repeat the following steps on all three Cat8Kv routers.

From the router CLI:

conf t
ip ssh pubkey-chain
 username admin
  key-string
   ssh-rsa AAAAB3NzaC1yc2EAAAADAQABAAACAQ... dcloud@ubuntu
  exit
 exit
end
write memory

⚠️ Important:

  • Paste the key on one single line
  • Do not add line breaks or extra spaces

docs.title: Step 4: Ensure SSH is Enabled on the Router
docs.text:
Still on the router CLI, ensure SSH prerequisites are configured:

conf t
ip domain name dmz.cisco.com
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
ip ssh version 2
end

If RSA keys already exist, the router may skip regeneration.

docs.title: Step 5: SSH from Ubuntu using the Key
docs.text:
From the Ubuntu host:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/c8kv_admin_key admin@198.18.6.11

You should log in without being prompted for a password.

docs.title: Step 6: Simplify Access using SSH Config
docs.text:
To avoid specifying the key and IP address every time, configure SSH aliases.

Edit the SSH config file:

nano ~/.ssh/config

Add the following entries:

Host c8kv-task-1
  HostName 198.18.6.11
  User admin
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/c8kv_admin_key

Host c8kv-task-2
  HostName 198.18.7.12
  User admin
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/c8kv_admin_key

Host c8kv-task-3
  HostName 198.18.8.13
  User admin
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/c8kv_admin_key

Now connect using a simple command:

ssh c8kv-task-1

docs.title: Sample Output
docs.text:
The authenticity of host '198.18.7.12 (198.18.7.12)' can't be established.
RSA key fingerprint is SHA256:A0uoPV8ZDbz2G3l5jAB9+/lFI7sX9hDyVRvInE9Uiq0.
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])? yes
Warning: Permanently added '198.18.7.12' (RSA) to the list of known hosts.

cat8Kv-task-2#

docs.title: Step 7: Execute Router Commands Directly from Ubuntu
docs.text:
You can now execute IOS-XE commands non-interactively from Ubuntu.

Example:

ssh c8kv-task-1 show ip int brief

docs.title: Sample Output

Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet4       198.18.1.11     YES NVRAM  up                    up
GigabitEthernet5       198.18.9.11     YES NVRAM  up                    up
GigabitEthernet6       198.18.6.11     YES NVRAM  up                    up
Connection to 198.18.6.11 closed by remote host.

✔️ At this point, passwordless SSH access is fully configured for all Cat8Kv routers, enabling fast CLI access and seamless automation from the Ubuntu host.

docs.title: Prerequisites: Router Preparation
docs.text:
Before starting Task-2, the C8000v router must be prepared for RESTCONF access and IOX App-Hosting.

Terraform uses RESTCONF APIs to manage App-Hosting resources, and the lab container images are unsigned, so signature verification must be disabled.

Run the following commands on the cat8Kv-task-2 SSH 198.18.1.12:

conf t
!
ip http secure-server
restconf
!
iox
 app-hosting signed-verification 
 !
 !
 !
 no app-hosting signed-verification 
!
end
wr mem

After completing the configuration, verify:

show ip http server status
show iox-service
show app-hosting infra

From the Lab Ubuntu VM, verify RESTCONF connectivity before running Terraform:

curl -k -u admin:C1sco12345 -H "Accept: application/yang-data+json" \
https://198.18.9.12/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/iox

Expected response: (It takes a few minutes)

{
  "Cisco-IOS-XE-native:iox": {}
}

Once these checks succeed, proceed to deployning the APP via Terraform.

docs.title: Step 6: Clone the App-Hosting Terraform Provider

Clone the Terraform provider repository from the Mgmt Ubuntu:

GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -o HostKeyAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa -o PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa' \
git clone ssh://lab@198.18.5.101/home/lab/terraform-provider-ciscoapphosting

docs.title: Step 7: Configure Terraform to Use the Local Provider
docs.text:
Terraform must be instructed to use the local provider instead of the public registry.

Create the Terraform CLI configuration file:

nano ~/.terraformrc

Paste the following content:

provider_installation {
  dev_overrides {
    "local/ciscoapphosting" = "/home/dcloud/terraform-provider-ciscoapphosting"
  }
  direct {}
}

Save and exit.

⚠️ A warning about provider development overrides is expected and normal.

mkdir ~/terraform-c8kv-apphosting

docs.title: 5.2 File: 01_vk_configmap.yaml (Remote Kubeconfig)
docs.text:
cat > 01_vk_configmap.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: remote-kubeconfig
  namespace: default
data:
  config: |
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Config
    clusters:
    - name: local-cluster
      cluster:
        certificate-authority: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc:443
    contexts:
    - name: default-context
      context:
        cluster: local-cluster
        user: pod-service-account
        namespace: default
    current-context: default-context
    users:
    - name: pod-service-account
      user:
        tokenFile: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
EOF

Apply:

kubectl apply -f 01_vk_configmap.yaml

Expected:

configmap/remote-kubeconfig created

docs.title: 5.3 File: 02_vk_deployment_config-r3.yaml (VK Device + Node Mapping)
docs.text:
cat > 02_vk_deployment_config_r3.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: vk-config-r3
  namespace: default
data:
  config.yaml: |
    device:
      name: cat8kv-router-r3
      driver: XE
      address: "198.18.8.13"
      port: 443
      username: admin
      password: C1sco12345
      tls:
        enabled: true
        insecureSkipVerify: true
      networking:
        dhcpEnabled: true
        virtualPortGroup: "0"
        defaultVRF: ""

    kubelet:
      node_name: "cat8kv-node-r3"
      namespace: ""
      update_interval: "30s"
      os: "Linux"
      node_internal_ip: "198.18.8.13"
EOF

Apply:

kubectl apply -f 02_vk_deployment_config_r3.yaml

Expected:

configmap/vk-config-r3 created

docs.title: 5.4 File: 03_vk_deployment_r3.yaml (Virtual Kubelet Deployment)
docs.text:
cat > 03_vk_deployment-r3.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cisco-virtual-kubelet-r3
  labels:
    app: cisco-virtual-kubelet-r3
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cisco-virtual-kubelet-r3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cisco-virtual-kubelet-r3
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/hostname: ubuntu-lab
      containers:
      - name: virtual-kubelet
        image: containers.dmz.cisco.com:5000/cisco-virtual-kubelet:1.0.0
        env:
        - name: KUBECONFIG
          value: "/etc/kubernetes/kubeconfig.yaml"
        volumeMounts:
        - name: kubeconfig-storage
          mountPath: "/etc/kubernetes"
          readOnly: true
        - name: vk-config-storage
          mountPath: "/etc/virtual-kubelet"
          readOnly: true
      volumes:
      - name: kubeconfig-storage
        configMap:
          name: remote-kubeconfig
          items:
          - key: "config"
            path: "kubeconfig.yaml"
      - name: vk-config-storage
        configMap:
          name: vk-config-r3
          items:
          - key: "config.yaml"
            path: "config.yaml"
EOF

Apply:

kubectl apply -f 03_vk_deployment-r3.yaml

Expected:

deployment.apps/cisco-virtual-kubelet-r3 created

docs.title: 5.5 File: 04_vk_pod_hello-app-r3.yaml (hello-app Pod on C8Kv)

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• fping – Fast ICMP Reachability Testing

  • 1. Check if a host is reachable (Ping scan)

The listed tools answer two very specific questions:

  • fping → Is the network path stable and fast?
  • dig → Is DNS resolving correctly and consistently?

They are often used before application troubleshooting.

docs.title: fping – Fast ICMP Reachability Testing
docs.text:
fping is an enhanced alternative to ping, designed for speed and scale.

Think of fping as:

“Can I test reachability to many hosts quickly and repeatedly?”

docs.title: 1. Basic reachability test
docs.text:
• Login to the Cat8Kv-Task-1 (ssh 198.18.1.11)
  • Connect to the swiss_knife container
app-hosting connect appid swiss_knife session /bin/bash

fping 8.8.8.8

What this shows

  • ICMP reachability
  • Immediate success or failure

docs.title: 2. Continuous packet loss and latency check
docs.text:
fping -c 10 -p 100 8.8.8.8

What this shows

  • Packet loss percentage
  • Min / avg / max latency

When to use

  • Intermittent connectivity issues
  • Path instability

docs.title: 3. Test multiple hosts at once
docs.text:
fping 1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8 9.9.9.9

Why this matters

  • Quickly compare reachability across paths
  • Identify localized issues

docs.title: dig – DNS Query and Resolution Testing
docs.text:
dig (Domain Information Groper) is a DNS inspection tool, not just a resolver.

Think of dig as:

“What DNS answer did I get, and where did it come from?”

docs.title: 1. Basic DNS lookup
docs.text:
dig google.com

What this shows

  • Query result
  • TTL
  • DNS server used

docs.title: 2. Query a specific DNS server
docs.text:
dig @8.8.8.8 google.com

What this shows

  • DNS response from a specific resolver
  • Useful for split-DNS troubleshooting

docs.title: 3. Query specific record types
docs.text:
dig google.com A
dig google.com AAAA

When to use

  • IPv4 vs IPv6 validation
  • Application connectivity issues

docs.title: 4. Short, script-friendly output
docs.text:
dig +short google.com

Why this matters

  • Clean output for automation
  • Easy comparison across resolvers

docs.title: nmap – Practical Examples
docs.text:
nmap is used before tools like nc, curl, or openssl to answer:

“What ports and services are exposed?”

docs.title: 1. Check if a host is reachable (Ping scan)
docs.text:
nmap -sn 8.8.8.8

What this does

  • Verifies basic host reachability
  • Uses ICMP and/or TCP probes

When to use

  • Confirm host is alive before deeper scans
  • Equivalent to router ping, but smarter

docs.title: 2. Scan specific TCP ports
docs.text:
nmap -p 22,80,443 198.18.101.5

What this tells you

  • Which ports are open / closed / filtered
  • Whether a service is reachable at all

Why this matters

If a port is closed here, nc and curl will fail too.

docs.title: 3. Fast scan of common ports
docs.text:
nmap -F 198.18.101.6

What this does

  • Scans top 100 common ports
  • Faster and safer than full scans

Typical use

  • Initial visibility check
  • Lab or pre-deployment validation

docs.title: How fping, dig and nmap fit in the flow
docs.text:
Tool Purpose fping Network reachability & stability dig DNS correctness nmap Port exposure nc TCP connectivity openssl TLS validation curl Application behavior

Key Takeways

  • ✅ Use fping to validate the path.
  • ✅ Use dig to validate the name resolution.
  • ✅ Use nmap to discover, not to troubleshoot application logic.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
In this task, you will use MTR (My Traceroute) from the Swiss-Knife container to analyze:

  • Network path visibility
  • Packet loss behavior
  • Latency trends across the path

This task focuses on real troubleshooting workflows, not command syntax memorization.

docs.title: Page Index
docs.text:
• Step 1: Baseline Path Test (ICMP)
  • Step 2: UDP-Based Path Test
  • Step 3: TCP-Based Path Test (Most Realistic)
  • Step 4: MTR Using Hostnames
  • How to Interpret MTR Output
  • Loss Interpretation Cheat Sheet
  • Key Takeaways

docs.title: Step 1: Baseline Path Test (ICMP)
docs.text:
Connect to Cat8Kv-Task-1 and access the Swiss-Knife container:

ssh 198.18.1.11
app-hosting connect appid swiss_knife session /bin/bash

Run a baseline ICMP MTR to a public destination:

mtr -r -n -c 20 8.8.8.8

Why this matters

  • Establishes basic reachability
  • Shows hop-by-hop latency
  • Acts as a baseline before deeper analysis

docs.title: MTR – Commonly Used Options
docs.text: Option Meaning Why it’s used -n Numeric output (no DNS lookup) Faster results, avoids DNS delays -r Report mode (no interactive UI) Script-friendly, clean output -c <count> Number of probes to send Control test duration -w Wide report format Prevents column wrapping, improves readability -T Use TCP probes Test application-like paths -u Use UDP probes Test non-ICMP traffic behavior

docs.title: Step 2: UDP-Based Path Test
docs.text: Run MTR using UDP to simulate application-like traffic.

docs.title: DNS-like traffic example
docs.text: mtr -r -n -u -P 53 8.8.8.8

docs.title: Voice / video / SLA-style traffic
docs.text:
mtr -r -n -u -P 16384 8.8.4.4

When to use UDP MTR

  • SD-WAN SLA validation
  • Voice / video path testing
  • Comparing ICMP vs policy-based paths

Note: UDP MTR does not send real application payloads. Some destinations may not respond — this is expected.

docs.title: Step 3: TCP-Based Path Test (Most Realistic)
docs.text: TCP MTR is the most reliable method in enterprise and cloud networks.

docs.title: HTTPS path test
docs.text: mtr -r -n -T -P 3000 198.18.5.101

docs.title: Alternate public target
docs.text:
mtr -r -n -T -P 443 208.67.220.220

Why TCP MTR is preferred

  • Traverses firewalls and NAT
  • Matches real application behavior
  • Aligns with SD-WAN and security policies

docs.title: Step 4: MTR Using Hostnames
docs.text:
You can also run MTR directly to hostnames:

mtr -r -T -P 443 www.cisco.com

What happens

  • DNS is resolved once
  • MTR traces to the resolved IP
  • Useful for SaaS and cloud troubleshooting

Best practice

dig www.google.com
mtr -r -n -T -P 443 <resolved-ip>

docs.title: Key interpretation rules
docs.text:
• Destination matters most

  • If destination shows 0% loss → path is healthy

  • ??? hops are normal

  • ICMP is often filtered or rate-limited

  • Latency trends matter

  • Gradual increase is normal

  • Sudden jump that continues indicates an issue

docs.title: Loss Interpretation Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Scenario Meaning Loss at one hop only Ignore Loss continues to destination Real problem ??? but destination reachable Normal behavior ICMP fails, TCP works ICMP filtered UDP fails, TCP works Expected

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• MTR provides path visibility, not application testing
  • TCP MTR is the most reliable in real networks
  • Ignore loss unless it reaches the destination
  • ??? hops are expected in SP and cloud environments

docs.title: 1. Basic Connectivity Test (GET)
docs.text:
• Login to the Cat8Kv-Task-1 (ssh 198.18.1.11)
  • Connect to the swiss_knife container
app-hosting connect appid swiss_knife session /bin/bash

curl https://www.google.com

docs.title: What this tells you
docs.text:
• DNS works (hostname resolved)
  • TCP/443 is reachable
  • TLS handshake completes
  • HTTP request/response succeeds

Tip: This prints the full HTML body (very noisy). Use -I or -v for troubleshooting.

docs.title: 2. Headers Only (-I) — “Is the web service up?”
docs.text: curl -I https://www.google.com

docs.title: What -I does
docs.text:
• Sends an HTTP HEAD request (or equivalent behavior depending on server/CDN)
  • Returns response headers only (no HTML body)
  • Fast and clean for reachability checks

docs.title: How to read the important headers
docs.text:
• HTTP/2 200 → request succeeded (HTTP status code 200 OK)
  • date: → server time when response was generated
  • server: gws → Google Web Server (useful to confirm which edge served you)
  • content-type: → response format (HTML / JSON / etc.)
  • cache-control: / expires: → caching behavior (important when troubleshooting “stale” pages)
  • set-cookie: → confirms the response was processed end-to-end (common for web apps)

  • alt-svc: h3=":443" → server advertises HTTP/3 (QUIC) availability on 443

  • Sample Output

swissknife:/root# curl -I https://www.google.com                                        
HTTP/2 200 
content-type: text/html; charset=ISO-8859-1
content-security-policy-report-only: object-src 'none';base-uri 'self';script-src 'nonce-xhH9ePIU8GyadCXkRymmXg' 'strict-dynamic' 'report-sample' 'unsafe-eval' 'unsafe-inline' https: http:;report-uri https://csp.withgoogle.com/csp/gws/other-hp
accept-ch: Sec-CH-Prefers-Color-Scheme
p3p: CP="This is not a P3P policy! See g.co/p3phelp for more info."
date: Sat, 17 Jan 2026 09:13:32 GMT
server: gws
x-xss-protection: 0
x-frame-options: SAMEORIGIN
expires: Sat, 17 Jan 2026 09:13:32 GMT
cache-control: private
set-cookie: AEC=AaJma5vSZ67DfW3zRxjvMo2OPJBX8M7gxDpdqY1bohAMbgk5hZ_6wZ6Fz90; expires=Thu, 16-Jul-2026 09:13:32 GMT; path=/; domain=.google.com; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=lax
set-cookie: __Secure-ENID=30.SE=FpIEnE9GiX6iQ5M1s8hTb4nGNsb_lEmS6nR85Ju0c1Ben9O29_OynUu0xIKR_uVSqwiH2HfSNCzmffZUH24JHakx5NgKhyKbPAj6c4WZZlpnbozXYGNv1jBVq2R2HK9XEVCTOaaaZmePf45ClvoHG50Fmt24WoorGqNm-bmCjeWvQeIT1zsQznzGH0NucilhsFz2f2irKyx6E4ncRhQQb5l1eg; expires=Wed, 17-Feb-2027 01:31:50 GMT; path=/; domain=.google.com; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=lax

swissknife:/root#

docs.title: 3. Verbose Mode (-v) — “Show me what fails and where”
docs.text: curl -v https://www.google.com

docs.title: What -v adds
docs.text:
Verbose mode prints the full transaction steps, which is exactly what you need when “it doesn’t work”:

  • DNS resolution results (A/AAAA records)
  • Which address curl tries first (IPv6 then IPv4)
  • TCP connect attempts and failures
  • TLS handshake details (TLS version, cipher, cert subject/issuer, validity)
  • ALPN negotiation (HTTP/2 vs HTTP/1.1)
  • Request headers sent + response headers received

Note: Curl tries IPv6 first and failed with Network unreachable, then fell back to IPv4 and succeeded. That’s a classic “no IPv6 routing” symptom in lab/enterprise networks.

docs.title: 4. Force a Specific IP While Keeping the Hostname (--resolve)
docs.text: curl -v https://8.8.8.8 --resolve www.google.com:443:8.8.8.8

docs.title: What this is doing
docs.text:
• --resolve injects a static DNS override inside curl:

  • “When connecting to www.google.com:443, use IP 8.8.8.8”

  • This is extremely useful to isolate:

  • DNS problems (bypass DNS completely)

  • Anycast / CDN behavior (force a specific edge)
  • Policy / routing differences to a specific destination IP

Lab use case: “DNS is broken” vs “path is blocked to the service”

  • If --resolve works but normal name doesn’t → DNS issue
  • If both fail → network / firewall / routing issue

docs.title: 5.1 Internal service example (Non 80 or 443 port)
docs.text:
curl -v http://198.18.101.6:3000

This is a perfect lab example of:

  • Port reachability
  • HTTP server identity (Server: lighttpd/1.4.82)

  • Valid HTTP status (200 OK)

  • Use your internal lab web app for 8080/8443 tests

docs.title: 6. About -k (Insecure TLS)
docs.text:
You used:

curl -vk https://example.com:8443

docs.title: What -k does
docs.text: • Skips TLS certificate verification (curl continues even if the CA chain is incomplete)

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Internal services using:

  • self-signed certs

  • private CA
  • incomplete chain
  • Quick validation: “Is TLS reachable at all?”

docs.title: When not to use it
docs.text:
• Production validation (it can hide real cert problems)

In your output, curl showed: SSL certificate verify result: unable to get local issuer certificate (20), continuing anyway. That’s exactly what -k is for in a lab.

docs.title: 7. Application Timing (Great for “slow app” complaints)
docs.text:
Command you ran:

curl -o /dev/null -s -w \
"DNS: %{time_namelookup}\nConnect: %{time_connect}\nTLS: %{time_appconnect}\nTTFB: %{time_starttransfer}\nTotal: %{time_total}\n" \
https://www.google.com

Example output :

DNS: 0.011500
Connect: 0.019673
TLS: 0.045948
TTFB: 0.087206
Total: 0.088797

docs.title: How to interpret these numbers
docs.text:
• DNS → time to resolve the hostname
  • Connect → time to establish TCP connection
  • TLS → time to complete TLS handshake (HTTPS only)
  • TTFB → Time To First Byte (server responsiveness + any middleboxes)
  • Total → full request time (until first response completes)

Troubleshooting clues

  • High DNS → resolver issue / reachability / latency to DNS
  • High Connect → routing / firewall / packet loss / congestion
  • High TLS → TLS inspection / slow handshake / CPU constraints
  • High TTFB with low Connect/TLS → server/backend slowness

docs.title: 8.1 Simple GET that returns JSON
docs.text: curl -s https://httpbin.org/get | head

docs.title: 8.2 GET with query parameters
docs.text: curl -s "https://httpbin.org/get?site=swissknife&tool=curl"

docs.title: 8.3 POST JSON body
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST https://httpbin.org/post \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"user":"test","pass":"test"}' | head

From the output notice that, httpbin is echoing back exactly what it received:

  • The data field shows the raw request body ({"user":"test","pass":"test"}), confirming the POST payload arrived intact.
  • The headers section reflects your request headers (for example Content-Type: application/json), confirming the request was processed as sent.

docs.title: 9. Recommended “Quick Checks” (Copy/Paste)
docs.text:
# 1) Is HTTPS reachable (headers only)?
curl -I https://www.google.com

# 2) Where does it fail (DNS / TCP / TLS / HTTP)?
curl -v https://www.google.com

# 3) Is it slow because of DNS, connect, TLS, or server?
curl -o /dev/null -s -w "DNS:%{time_namelookup}\nConnect:%{time_connect}\nTLS:%{time_appconnect}\nTTFB:%{time_starttransfer}\nTotal:%{time_total}\n" https://www.google.com

# 4) Is this a DNS problem or a routing/firewall problem?
curl -v https://1.1.1.1 --resolve example.com:443:1.1.1.1

docs.title: 10. wget — File Download + Availability Checks
docs.text: wget is great when you want to download files, validate reachability, or test stability (resume support).

docs.title: 10.1 Basic download
docs.text:
wget -O- --no-check-certificate https://hel1-speed.hetzner.com/100MB.bin | head -c 10485760 > 10MB.bin
<hetzner.com/100MB.bin | head -c 10485760 > 10MB.bin

What to look for:

  • DNS resolution + connect success
  • Steady download progress (up to 10 Meg)
  • File saved locally (good for throughput / path validation)
  • Delete the file to make sure we have space for future tasks
rm 10MB.bin

docs.title: 10.2 Headers / existence check only - --spider
docs.text:
wget --spider https://www.google.com

What it does :

  • Does NOT download the page/file
  • Sends an HTTP request and checks the response
  • You got 200 OK + “Remote file exists…” → the URL is reachable and responding

Use case:

  • Quick “is it up?” check without pulling content (great in automation and troubleshooting)

docs.title: 10.3 Force IPv4 vs IPv6 — -4 / -6
docs.text:
IPv4 forced :

wget -4 https://www.google.com

IPv6 forced :

wget -6 https://www.google.com

What this tells you:

  • -4 forces wget to use A records (IPv4) only
  • -6 forces wget to use AAAA records (IPv6) only
  • Your -6 failure Network unreachable confirms no IPv6 routing from that container/network, even though DNS can resolve IPv6 addresses

Use case:

  • Quickly prove whether an issue is IPv6 reachability vs application/DNS
  • Useful when apps behave differently over v4/v6, or when dual-stack policy is involved

docs.title: 11. HTTPie – API Calls
docs.text:
• HTTPie does the same job as curl.
  • It presents the request and response in a more human-readable format (JSON-first, cleaner defaults).

docs.title: 11.1 Basic GET
docs.text:
Use --verify=no : The container doesn’t have the full CA chain installed

http --verify=no https://httpbin.org/get

What you’ll see echoed back

  • Your source IP/headers (in JSON)
  • Any query params you pass
  • Request metadata (helps validate what the app “sees”)

docs.title: 11.2 Headers only
docs.text:
http --verify=no -h https://httpbin.org/get

Use case

  • Confirm HTTP status, Content-Type, and server headers without printing the body.

docs.title: 11.3 Verbose
docs.text:
http --verify=no --verbose https://httpbin.org/get
  • HTTPie prints the request headers first (),
  • It attempts the TLS connection and fails unless --verify=no is used.

docs.title: 11.4 POST JSON
docs.text:
http --verify=no POST https://httpbin.org/post user=test pass=test123

Verification

  • httpbin will echo your payload back in the response as JSON (similar idea to curl’s data/json echo).

docs.title: 12. Comparing curl, wget, and httpie
docs.text: Tool Best For curl Deep troubleshooting, timing, TLS wget File downloads, availability httpie APIs, JSON, readability

docs.title: 13. Tool Selection Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
Question Tool Is host reachable? ping What path is used? mtr Is app reachable? curl Is DNS working? dig Is file accessible? wget Is API behaving correctly? httpie

socat is a versatile data-transfer utility that can relay traffic between sockets, files, and processes.

In this lab, socat is used to validate connectivity, simulate services, proxy traffic, generate traffic, transfer files, and inspect application flows running inside containers.

Here’s a clean, lab-ready section you can drop immediately after the intro. It’s written in the same neutral, instructional tone you’ve been using elsewhere.

docs.title: Accessing the Lab Containers
docs.text: For the following demonstrations, two Swiss-Knife containers are used. Each container is deployed on a separate Catalyst 8000v (C8Kv) router using App-Hosting.

docs.title: Lab Setup Overview
docs.text: Component Management IP Container IP cat8kv-task-1 198.18.1.11 198.18.100.5 cat8kv-task-2 198.18.1.12 198.18.101.5

docs.title: Step 1: SSH to both the Routers directly from the PC
docs.text: Connect to the cat8kv-task-1 and cat8kv-task-2 hosting the swiss knife container.

docs.title: Step 2: Access the Swiss-Knife Container
docs.text:
Once logged into the router CLI, connect to the container shell:

app-hosting connect appid swiss_knife session /bin/bash

You will now be inside the Swiss-Knife container and can run socat commands directly.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• All socat commands in this document are executed inside the Swiss-Knife container
  • Container IPs are reachable end-to-end and are used for traffic generation, proxying, and inspection
  • Multiple terminal sessions are recommended when running listeners and clients simultaneously

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Start a lightweight TCP service to receive and display incoming data.

docs.title: Command (Listener > Cat8Kv-task-1 > container)
docs.text: socat -v TCP-LISTEN:8080,reuseaddr,fork STDOUT

docs.title: Test (Client > Cat8Kv-task-2 > container)
docs.text: echo "hello from client" | socat - TCP:198.18.100.5:8080

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: Incoming TCP connections are accepted and payloads are printed to the terminal.

docs.title: Use Case 2: TCP Port Forwarding (Proxy) + Verbose/Debug
Objective
docs.text:
Forward traffic from a local TCP port to a remote service while logging connection and payload details.

We will SSH on port 9000 to the container's IP which will be redirected on port 22 to the router (cat8Kv-task-1) IP.

docs.title: Command (Cat8Kv-task-1 > container)
docs.text: socat -d -d -v TCP-LISTEN:9000,reuseaddr,fork TCP:198.18.100.1:22

docs.title: Optional (Hex dump of payloads)
docs.text: socat -d -d -v -x TCP-LISTEN:9000,reuseaddr,fork TCP:198.18.100.1:22

docs.title: Test (Lab Ubuntu)
docs.text:
ssh -p 9000 admin@198.18.100.5

Provide the router's password when prompted.

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: Traffic received on port 9000 on the swiss_knife is forwarded to the cat8Kv-task-1 router on port 22, while socat logs connection lifecycle and payloads.

docs.title: Use Case 3: UDP Send and Receive (IPv4 Explicit)
Objective
docs.text: Generate and receive UDP traffic between endpoints.

docs.title: Receiver (Cat8Kv-task-1 > container)
docs.text: socat -d -d -v UDP4-LISTEN:5000,reuseaddr,fork STDOUT

docs.title: Sender (Cat8Kv-task-2 > container)
docs.text: echo "UDP Test From Cat8Kv-task-2 $(date)" | socat - UDP4:198.18.100.5:5000

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: UDP payloads are received and displayed in real time.

docs.title: Use Case 4: File Transfer Over TCP (TXT, One-Way)
Objective
docs.text: Transfer a text file between containers using a raw TCP connection.

docs.title: Receiver (Cat8Kv-task-1 > container)
docs.text: socat -d -d -u TCP4-LISTEN:6000,reuseaddr,fork OPEN:/tmp/received.txt,creat,trunc

docs.title: Sender (Cat8Kv-task-2 > container)
docs.text:
printf "hello-from-R1\n" > /tmp/send.txt
socat -d -d -u FILE:/tmp/send.txt TCP4:198.18.100.5:6000

docs.title: Verify (on receiver)
docs.text: cat /tmp/received.txt

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: The receiver writes the file to /tmp/received.txt successfully.

docs.title: Use Case 5: Inline Traffic Inspection Using Two Router Containers
Objective
docs.text: Inspect application traffic inline while forwarding it between two router-hosted containers.

docs.title: Lab Topology
docs.text:
• Cat8Kv-task-1 Container (Proxy / Inspection): 198.18.100.5
  • Cat8Kv-task-2 Container (Backend Service): 198.18.101.5
  • Lab Ubuntu (Client): 198.18.9.100

docs.title: Step 1: Start Backend HTTP Server on R2 Container
docs.text:
On Cat8Kv-task-2 container (198.18.101.5):

python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 0.0.0.0

docs.title: Step 2: Start Inline Inspection Proxy on R1 Container
docs.text:
On Cat8Kv-task-1 container (198.18.100.5):

socat -d -d -v TCP-LISTEN:8081,reuseaddr,fork TCP:198.18.101.5:8080

docs.title: Optional (Hex dump of payloads)
docs.text: socat -d -d -v -x TCP-LISTEN:8081,reuseaddr,fork TCP:198.18.101.5:8080

docs.title: Step 3: Generate Traffic from Lab Ubuntu
docs.text:
From Lab Ubuntu (198.18.9.100):

curl -v http://198.18.100.5:8081/

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
• Ubuntu receives the HTTP response from Cat8Kv-task-2 Container via Cat8Kv-task-1 Container
  • Cat8Kv-task-1 Container prints request/response payloads due to -v (and hex if -x)
  • Cat8Kv-task-2 Container logs incoming requests via the python HTTP server

docs.title: Task 8: kcat (Kafka CAT) Connectivity & Message Flow
docs.text:
⬅️ Back to Main Menu

kcat is a lightweight CLI tool to validate Kafka connectivity, topics, and message flow without needing to install a full Kafka client stack on the router.

Lab context - Kafka Broker is running on Mgmt Ubuntu 1 (198.18.5.101:9092) - You will run kcat from the Swiss-Knife container on cat8Kv-task-1

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• Step 1: Connect to the Swiss-Knife container
  • Step 2: Validate broker connectivity and metadata
  • Step 3: List topics (read-only check)
  • Step 4: Produce messages to a topic
  • Step 5: Consume messages from a topic
  • Troubleshooting quick tips

docs.title: Step 1: Connect to the Swiss-Knife container
docs.text:
On cat8Kv-task-1:

app-hosting connect appid swiss_knife session /bin/bash

docs.title: Step 2: Validate broker connectivity and metadata
docs.text:
This confirms: / - TCP reachability to the broker / - Kafka protocol handshake works / - You can retrieve cluster/topic metadata

kcat -b 198.18.5.101:9092 -L

Expected result (example)

Metadata for all topics (from broker 1: 198.18.5.101:9092/1):
 1 brokers:
  broker 1 at 198.18.5.101:9092 (controller)
 1 topics:
  topic "netops-test" with 1 partitions:
    partition 0, leader 1, replicas: 1, isrs: 1

docs.title: Step 3: List topics (read-only check)
docs.text:
Use this when: / - An application reports “topic not found” / - You want to validate you are pointing to the correct environment/broker

kcat -b 198.18.5.101:9092 -L | grep -i topic

docs.title: Step 4: Produce messages to a topic
docs.text:
Send a single test message from the container to Kafka:

echo "hello-from-cat8kv-task-1" | kcat -b 198.18.5.101:9092 -t netops-test -P

This should run withut any output or error, the message is received by the broker What this demonstrates:

  • The router/container can publish events (logs/telemetry/test messages)
  • The end-to-end path to Kafka is working

docs.title: Step 5: Consume messages from a topic
docs.text:
Start a consumer to verify that messages are arriving.

kcat -b 198.18.5.101:9092 -t netops-test -C

Notes: - This command runs continuously. / - The message sent in the previous step can be seen here / - Press Ctrl+C to stop the consumer.

docs.title: Troubleshooting quick tips
docs.text:
• If kcat -L times out: verify reachability (ping, tracepath, ACLs), and confirm the broker IP/port.
  • If produce works but consume shows nothing: confirm you are consuming the same topic, and that the producer actually published (use -C -o beginning to read from the start).
kcat -b 198.18.5.101:9092 -t netops-test -C -o beginning

docs.title: Step 5: Initialize MRTG and Generate Graphs
docs.text:
mrtg /opt/mrtg/mrtg.cfg --check

rm -f /opt/mrtg/html/*.log /opt/mrtg/html/*.old

Run MRTG multiple times to generate baseline data:

mrtg /opt/mrtg/mrtg.cfg
mrtg /opt/mrtg/mrtg.cfg
mrtg /opt/mrtg/mrtg.cfg

Generate the index page:

indexmaker /opt/mrtg/mrtg.cfg > /opt/mrtg/html/index.html

docs.title: Step 6: Start Web Server (lighttpd)
docs.text:
Create config:

cat > /etc/lighttpd/lighttpd.conf <<'EOF'
server.document-root = "/opt/mrtg/html"
server.port = 8080
server.bind = "0.0.0.0"
dir-listing.activate = "enable"
mimetype.assign = (
  ".html" => "text/html",
  ".png"  => "image/png",
  ".css"  => "text/css"
)
EOF

Start in background:

lighttpd -f /etc/lighttpd/lighttpd.conf &

docs.title: Step 7: Enable Continuous Polling (Cron every 5 minutes)
docs.text:
Edit crontab:

crontab -e

Insert, save and exit :

*/5 * * * * /usr/bin/mrtg /opt/mrtg/mrtg.cfg --logging /opt/mrtg/mrtg.log

Start cron and verify:

crond
ps | grep crond
crontab -l

docs.title: Step 8: View the Graphs
docs.text:
RDP to the lab desktop:

RDP to 198.18.1.20

Open browser:

http://198.18.102.5:8080/index.html

You should see:

  • Task-1: Gig5/Gig6 traffic + CPU + Memory
  • Task-2: Gig5/Gig6 traffic + CPU + Memory
  • Task-3: Gig5/Gig6 traffic + CPU + Memory

docs.title: Determine Interface Index Mapping (if needed)
docs.text:
To verify which ifIndex maps to which interface:

snmpwalk -v2c -c public <router-ip> 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2

Example:

  • ifDescr.2 = GigabitEthernet5
  • ifDescr.3 = GigabitEthernet6

docs.title: Optional Traffic Generation with iPerf3 (Observation Step)
docs.text: To make the MRTG graphs more meaningful, we will now generate traffic between routers and observe the impact on the interface graphs.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• Generate controlled traffic between Cat8Kv-Task-1 and Cat8Kv-Task-2
  • Validate that MRTG graphs correctly reflect real traffic changes
  • Reinforce the concept of poll-based monitoring

docs.title: Optional Step 1: Move to iPerf3 Traffic Generation Task
docs.text:
At this point, pause the MRTG task and switch to the iPerf3 lab task.

In the iPerf3 task:

  • Configure Cat8Kv-Task-1 as the iPerf server
  • Configure Cat8Kv-Task-2 as the iPerf client
  • Run sustained traffic for 2–5 minutes

(Detailed steps are covered in the dedicated iPerf3 lab section.)

docs.title: Optional Step 2: Return to MRTG and Observe the Impact
docs.text:
After traffic generation:

  1. Wait 5–10 minutes (to allow multiple MRTG polling cycles)
  2. Refresh the MRTG web page:
http://198.18.102.5:8080/index.html

  1. Observe:

  2. Increased inbound/outbound traffic on:

    • GigabitEthernet5
    • GigabitEthernet6

    • Corresponding changes in:

    • CPU utilization

    • Memory usage (minor fluctuations expected)

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
MRTG provides a historical, trend-based view of network behavior, making it ideal for validating traffic patterns over time, rather than instantaneous troubleshooting.
